The geometric argument requires observations of angles and terrestrial distances.
Rainfall and river-flow estimates allowed an explicit comparison of water input and output.
Steno’s anatomical comparison of shark teeth with tongue stones supported an organic interpretation of those fossils.
Relations among deposited, tilted, and eroded layers expose sequences requiring substantial time.
Interpreting fossils as former life made rock sequences records of a past biological world. This is a conceptual connection to deep time.
Hutton’s account of long geological histories informed Lyell’s later process-based synthesis.
Layered rock relationships provide historical observations that modern geological processes can help explain.
Comparing present glaciers with older landforms supports inference to former glaciation. This is a methodological connection.
Discrepancies in geodetic observations created the problem of gravitational compensation.
Gravitational balance supplies the physical framework for compensation models.
Combining repeated ship observations made persistent patterns of currents and winds identifiable.
Instrumental recordings replace only qualitative descriptions with comparable measurements of motion.
Radioactive dating supplied numerical estimates for the long histories previously inferred from rock relationships.
Matching fossil distributions on separated continents were part of Wegener’s evidence for former connections.
Ancient glacial traces in now-separated regions supplied evidence that their past geographic arrangement differed.
Organism–environment relationships can be extended to the movement of elements through living and nonliving reservoirs.
Accounting for chemical elements makes material transfers through the biosphere intelligible. This is a conceptual dependency.
Tansley’s ecosystem concept developed within debates about the units and physical context of ecological study.
Water exchange exemplifies the physical connections that ecosystem analysis includes alongside organisms.
Seismic arrivals provided the observations from which Lehmann inferred an inner core.
The radiative effect of carbon dioxide provides the physical link from increased concentration to warming.
Explaining repeated glacial advances and retreats motivated calculations of long-term orbital forcing.
Continuous calculations of orbital geometry and insolation underlie quantitative astronomical climate models.
The disagreement between polar-wander paths could be interpreted by allowing continents to move relative to one another.
Sensitive measurements of weak remanent magnetization made continental comparisons possible.
Moving oceanic crust supplied a way for continents to travel without plowing through a fixed seafloor.
The broader growth of systematic oceanography enabled exploration and mapping of ocean basins. This is a field-level conceptual connection.
Creation and removal of oceanic crust became part of a coherent model of moving plates.
Magnetic patterns and reversals supplied tests of ocean-floor movement incorporated into the plate synthesis.
Earthquake locations and motion directions constrained plate boundaries and relative movements.
Rigid motions on a sphere provide the mathematical description of relative plate movements.
Radiative transfer and atmospheric absorption are essential physical ingredients of climate calculations.
Conservation and transport of heat constrain how atmospheric temperature responds to radiation and convection.
Time-dependent physical processes are represented by equations that can be solved or approximated numerically.
Different wavelength responses allow multispectral measurements to distinguish materials and surface conditions.
Reaction mechanisms and rates explain how chlorine can catalytically remove ozone.
The breakup and rearrangement of molecules connects CFC decomposition with reactive chlorine chemistry.
Coupling organisms with their physical environment supplies one part of a planetary systems perspective.
Elemental transfers connect living systems with atmosphere, oceans, land, and rock.
Physical climate models provide a way to investigate interactions and feedbacks across planetary components.
Repeated global observations make changes across coupled Earth components measurable.
Ocean transport connects heat and material exchanges over large distances and timescales.
Predictable radioactive decay supplied a physical clock for assigning numerical ages to suitable minerals.
